theme: Bethlehem’s ruler; future peace among the nations
readingInstruction: Read Micah 4:1-5:15. After the judgments of chapters 1 to 3, the tone changes to hope. Read the vision of the mountain of the LORD, then slow down at 5:2, the promise of a ruler from Bethlehem.
settingTheScene: These two chapters are the hinge of Micah. After the threat of destruction, God shows what he will do beyond it: gather the nations to Zion, bring peace, and raise up a ruler who will shepherd his people. Verse 5:2 is one of the best known prophecies of the coming Messiah, and it was already being quoted by the scribes in Jesus’ day.
observation: “It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains” (4:1).
“Many nations shall come, and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD” (4:2).
“They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation” (4:3).
“But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (4:4).
“And you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel” (5:2).
“Whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (5:2).
“And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD” (5:4).
interpretation:
Micah 4:1-3 is almost identical to Isaiah 2:2-4, a sign of how important this vision was to the prophets. In the last days, the temple mount will be exalted, and the nations will come, not as conquered subjects but as willing learners. “He may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.” The word of the LORD will go out from Jerusalem. And as a result, the nations will stop fighting. Weapons become farming tools. Everyone sits under their own vine and fig tree, a picture of security and peace.

What makes this vision striking is its setting. It follows the destruction of chapter 3. The very hill that will be plowed like a field becomes the highest mountain. God does not give up on his plan. Out of ruins he builds a worldwide kingdom.

The prophet admits that suffering comes first. Israel will go to Babylon, “writhing like a woman in labor,” but there God will rescue and redeem them. Their enemies think they are finished, but “they do not know the thoughts of the LORD.”

Then comes 5:2. Bethlehem was a tiny village, “too little to be among the clans of Judah.” Yet from it will come the ruler of Israel. God consistently chooses the small things. David had been the youngest son from this same town. And the ruler’s origin is “from of old, from ancient days,” language that points beyond a merely human king. He will “shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD,” and “they shall dwell secure, for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth.” And the key line: “And he shall be their peace.”

He does not just bring peace. He is peace. The final part of the chapter promises the purging of idols and the removal of every false security. The kingdom is not built on horses and chariots but on the LORD.
connection: When the magi came to Jerusalem asking where the king of the Jews was born, the chief priests and scribes quoted Micah 5:2 (Matthew 2:1-6). Jesus is the shepherd (John 10:11) and “our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD are fulfilled in the gathering of the church from every tribe (Revelation 7:9). Isaiah 9:6-7 names the coming child “Prince of Peace.”
application:
Reread Micah 5:2 and thank God for Bethlehem, a small place that held the greatest gift.

Notice where God works through things that seem small and overlooked, including in your own life.

Pray for peace in a specific conflict, and for the day when swords become plowshares.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the ruler from little Bethlehem.
Ask him to shepherd you in his strength.
Ask him to be your peace.
